title: I Closed a Business a Year Ago The Cleanup Hasn't Stopped
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder reflects on the ongoing aftermath of closing a business -- payroll errors, vendor balances, legal cleanup, and tax amendments that keep arriving on their own schedule -- and the emotional cost that comes with each new piece of cleanup. The article explores how a single tax notice can erase the memory of what actually went well: employees who landed well, clients who were transitioned thoughtfully, businesses her former staff went on to start. She introduces a house-flipping metaphor: there is no clean close on any of it -- one house photographs beautifully while another is mid-demolition, and that is not a sign you got it wrong. The central leadership insight is about narrative control: not letting the ongoing cleanup rewrite the whole story.
points: Major decisions -- including the decision to close a business -- do not have clean end dates; the cleanup arrives on its own schedule and can reopen the emotional wound of the decision each time a new piece surfaces.

When a tax notice lands, the mind defaults to the wreckage -- as if the good never happened and the only real thing is who was let down -- a cognitive distortion that narrative discipline must actively resist.

The closing was the right call, and it still cost people: holding both truths simultaneously, without letting the cost erase the rightness of the call, is a specific leadership capacity that must be practiced.

The house-flipping metaphor reframes ongoing cleanup as expected, not pathological: you buy the mess on purpose, spend months turning it into something valuable, and the next project is already in mid-demo while the previous one closes.

Responsible closure includes active stewardship after the decision: sending referrals to former employees who started businesses, setting up partnerships so clients land in good hands -- the ethical obligation does not end at the announcement.
quotes: Months after I closed my company, someone who used to work for me is untangling a tax mess they didn't cause because of something that happened on my watch.

Every one of these reopens the same wound and it goes deeper than the paperwork. People trusted me to handle the basics, and this time I didn't. And underneath the guilt is something I don't say openly much: the shame of closing a business in public, at this stage of my life, not knowing if I let down people who didn't deserve it, and wondering if I just failed.

The strange thing is how fast I forget all of that. One tax notice lands and my mind goes straight to the wreckage, like the good never happened and the only thing that was ever real is who I let down. The closing was the right call, and it still cost people I cared about.
I'm just trying to stop letting the cleanup rewrite the whole story.

What I'm making peace with is that there's no clean close on any of it. You finish one thing and move on, good things actually start happening, and somewhere behind you there's still a mess that needs tending. That's not a sign you got it wrong." Page 1
